Statistical Optimal Transport

Optimal transport is rarely evaluated on population measures directly. In machine learning and statistics, the inputs are usually empirical laws, histograms, simulated particles or minibatches, and the central question is therefore no longer only how to compute OT, but how OT behaves as a random estimator. This chapter studies this statistical layer: qualitative consistency of empirical measures, non-asymptotic sample-complexity rates, and asymptotic bias--variance decompositions for exact and regularized transport costs.

This statistical convergence is conceptually different from the algorithmic convergence studied in the previous chapter. There the marginals and the temperature were fixed and one asked how Sinkhorn iterates approach a regularized optimizer. Here the number of samples grows, the empirical measures themselves move, and the regularization parameter may either remain fixed or be sent to zero. The resulting picture explains why exact OT is statistically expensive in high intrinsic dimension, why fixed-temperature Sinkhorn has smoother parametric fluctuations, and why approximating exact OT with entropy always involves a bias--variance tradeoff.

Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem¶

Before discussing sample complexity, it is useful to separate consistency from rates. If X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ are i.i.d. samples with common law α\alphaα, the associated empirical measure is the random probability measure

α^n:=1n∑i=1nδXi.\hat\alpha_n \eqdef \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}.α^n​:=n1​i=1∑n​δXi​​.
(1)

The ordinary law of large numbers says that empirical averages converge to expectations. In measure language this means that α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ converges weakly toward α\alphaα, because testing α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ against a bounded continuous function φ\varphiφ gives the sample average n−1∑iφ(Xi)n^{-1}\sum_i\varphi(X_i)n−1∑i​φ(Xi​). Wasserstein distances strengthen this statement by also recording moment convergence. Thus, if α\alphaα has a finite ppp-th moment, the empirical law converges to α\alphaα in Wp\Wass_pWp​, almost surely and in ppp-th mean in the sense that EWp(α^n,α)p→0\mathbb E\Wass_p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)^p\to0EWp​(α^n​,α)p→0. This is the qualitative consistency statement behind empirical OT plug-in estimators: empirical transport distances converge to their population counterparts once the sampled laws themselves converge in Wasserstein distance. It says nothing yet about the speed, which is the topic of Sample Complexity.

Central-Limit Fluctuations¶

The previous proposition is a law-of-large-numbers statement: a random empirical measure converges to the law that generated it. The central limit theorem describes a different, fluctuation-scale limit. As recalled in Remark Remark: Central limit theorem, if (Xi)i≥1(X_i)_{i\geq1}(Xi​)i≥1​ are centered i.i.d. random vectors with identity covariance, the law of n−1/2∑iXin^{-1/2}\sum_i X_in−1/2∑i​Xi​ converges weakly toward a Gaussian. Equivalently, if α\alphaα is the common law of the XiX_iXi​, this law is the rescaled convolution (D1/n)♯α∗n(D_{1/\sqrt n})_\sharp\alpha^{*n}(D1/n​​)♯​α∗n. Wasserstein distances make this qualitative convergence quantitative. The next result is a W1\Wass_1W1​ form of the Berry--Esseen theorem: it controls the error uniformly over all 1-Lipschitz test functions.

Sample Complexity¶

This section separates two statistical regimes. Exact OT resolves geometry at all spatial scales and pays rates controlled by the metric entropy, hence by the intrinsic dimension, of the support. Fixed-temperature Sinkhorn divergences smooth the dual potentials and recover parametric fluctuations, at the price of regularization bias.

The previous section proves qualitative convergence of empirical laws. The sample-complexity question is how fast this convergence happens. The sample complexity of unregularized OT suffers from the curse of dimensionality, but the relevant dimension is geometric. If the distributions are supported on a regular lower-dimensional set, for instance a d′d'd′-dimensional submanifold of Rd\RR^dRd, the empirical rate is governed by d′d'd′ rather than by the ambient dimension ddd. In the high-dimensional regime for Wp\Wass_pWp​, namely d′>2pd'>2pd′>2p, this gives the characteristic rate n−1/d′n^{-1/d'}n−1/d′. Exact OT is therefore dimension-adaptive: it sees the intrinsic dimension of the data support through its covering numbers Dudley, 1969Weed & Bach, 2019. Entropic regularization changes a different aspect of the picture: for a fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, Sinkhorn divergences have parametric n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 statistical rates, although the constant deteriorates when ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0 Genevay et al., 2019Bigot et al., 2019. Related two-sample-testing viewpoints are developed in Ramdas et al., 2017, and the large-ϵ\epsilonϵ kernel limit connects to classical MMD tests Gretton et al., 2012.

show_book_figure("sinkhorn-bias-variance-tradeoff")

Empirical fluctuations in dimensions three and six. For each sample size nnn, two independent empirical measures are drawn from the same standard Gaussian law. Exact OT follows a slower dimension-dependent scale, while MMD and the fixed-ϵ\epsilonϵ Sinkhorn divergence behave closer to the parametric n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 guide. This is a statistical illustration, not a solver benchmark.

Proposition: Empirical OT has Intrinsic-Dimension Value Rates

Let α\alphaα and β\betaβ be probability distributions with densities bounded above and below on [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d, and let α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ and β^m\hat\beta_mβ^​m​ be independent empirical measures. For d>2pd>2pd>2p, the expected empirical error for estimating the two-sample distance obeys

E∣Wp(α^n,β^m)−Wp(α,β)∣≲n−1/d+m−1/d.\mathbb E \abs{ \Wass_p(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m) - \Wass_p(\alpha,\beta) } \lesssim n^{-1/d}+m^{-1/d}.E∣∣​Wp​(α^n​,β^​m​)−Wp​(α,β)∣∣​≲n−1/d+m−1/d.
(10)

The exponent changes in low dimension, but the important message is that exact OT deteriorates with the intrinsic dimension of the support rather than necessarily with the ambient dimension. More generally, if the measures are supported on a compact set with regular d′d'd′-dimensional volume growth, so that covering numbers at scale rrr are of order r−d′r^{-d'}r−d′, the same estimate holds with ddd replaced by d′d'd′ when d′>2pd'>2pd′>2p. This includes smooth compact d′d'd′-dimensional submanifolds with densities bounded above and below with respect to their volume measure.

Proof Sketch

By the triangle inequality,

∣Wp(α^n,β^m)−Wp(α,β)∣≤Wp(α^n,α)+Wp(β^m,β).\abs{\Wass_p(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\Wass_p(\alpha,\beta)} \leq \Wass_p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha) + \Wass_p(\hat\beta_m,\beta).∣∣​Wp​(α^n​,β^​m​)−Wp​(α,β)∣∣​≤Wp​(α^n​,α)+Wp​(β^​m​,β).
(11)

For the one-sample term, partition [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d into dyadic cubes. At scale 2−j2^{-j}2−j, empirical mass fluctuations over the cells are of order n−1/22jd/2n^{-1/2}2^{jd/2}n−1/22jd/2, while moving this excess mass inside cells costs 2−j2^{-j}2−j. Summing the multiscale contributions up to the scale where the expected number of samples per cell is order one gives 2−J2^{-J}2−J with 2Jd≃n2^{Jd}\simeq n2Jd≃n, hence n−1/dn^{-1/d}n−1/d. On a support with d′d'd′-dimensional metric entropy, the same chaining argument uses covers with O(2jd′)O(2^{jd'})O(2jd′) cells at scale 2−j2^{-j}2−j, hence the balancing scale is 2Jd′≃n2^{Jd'}\simeq n2Jd′≃n and the rate is n−1/d′n^{-1/d'}n−1/d′. Matching lower bounds follow from packing arguments Dudley, 1969Fournier & Guillin, 2015Weed & Bach, 2019.

Proposition: MMD has a Parametric Value Rate

Let kkk be a bounded positive definite kernel with RKHS Hk\mathcal H_kHk​, and define

MMD⁡k(α,β):=∥∫k(x,⋅)  d(α−β)(x)∥Hk.\operatorname{MMD}_k(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \norm{ \int k(x,\cdot)\,\d(\alpha-\beta)(x) }_{\mathcal H_k}.MMDk​(α,β):=∥∥​∫k(x,⋅)d(α−β)(x)∥∥​Hk​​.
(12)

If α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ and β^m\hat\beta_mβ^​m​ are independent empirical measures, then

E∣MMD⁡k(α^n,β^m)−MMD⁡k(α,β)∣≤κ(1n+1m)\mathbb E \abs{ \operatorname{MMD}_k(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m) - \operatorname{MMD}_k(\alpha,\beta) } \leq \kappa\left(\frac1{\sqrt n}+\frac1{\sqrt m}\right)E∣∣​MMDk​(α^n​,β^​m​)−MMDk​(α,β)∣∣​≤κ(n​1​+m​1​)
(13)

when k(x,x)≤κ2k(x,x)\leq\kappa^2k(x,x)≤κ2.

Proof

Let Φ(x)=k(x,⋅)\Phi(x)=k(x,\cdot)Φ(x)=k(x,⋅) be the feature map and mα=EΦ(X)m_\alpha=\mathbb E\Phi(X)mα​=EΦ(X). The reverse triangle inequality gives

∣MMD⁡k(α^n,β^m)−MMD⁡k(α,β)∣≤MMD⁡k(α^n,α)+MMD⁡k(β^m,β).\abs{ \operatorname{MMD}_k(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m) - \operatorname{MMD}_k(\alpha,\beta) } \leq \operatorname{MMD}_k(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha) + \operatorname{MMD}_k(\hat\beta_m,\beta).∣∣​MMDk​(α^n​,β^​m​)−MMDk​(α,β)∣∣​≤MMDk​(α^n​,α)+MMDk​(β^​m​,β).

EMMD⁡k(α^n,α)2=1nE∥Φ(X)−mα∥Hk2=1n(Ek(X,X)−Ek(X,X′)).\mathbb E\operatorname{MMD}_k(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)^2 = \frac1n \mathbb E\norm{\Phi(X)-m_\alpha}_{\mathcal H_k}^2 = \frac1n \left( \mathbb E k(X,X)-\mathbb E k(X,X') \right).EMMDk​(α^n​,α)2=n1​E∥Φ(X)−mα​∥Hk​2​=n1​(Ek(X,X)−Ek(X,X′)).
(15)

Jensen’s inequality and k(x,x)≤κ2k(x,x)\leq\kappa^2k(x,x)≤κ2 give the displayed bound.

Proposition: Sinkhorn Divergences Interpolate the Rates

Assume α\alphaα and β\betaβ are supported in a compact subset of Rd\RR^dRd and the cost is smooth. For fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, debiased Sinkhorn divergences satisfy representative empirical bounds of the form

E∣L‾cϵ(α^n,β^m)−L‾cϵ(α,β)∣≤Cc,dϵ−d/2(1n+1m),\mathbb E \abs{ \overline{\mathcal L}_c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m) - \overline{\mathcal L}_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) } \leq C_{c,d}\epsilon^{-d/2} \left( \frac1{\sqrt n}+\frac1{\sqrt m} \right),E∣∣​Lcϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)−Lcϵ​(α,β)∣∣​≤Cc,d​ϵ−d/2(n​1​+m​1​),
(16)

up to constants and exponents depending on the precise smoothness class and support diameter. Thus regularization removes the n−1/dn^{-1/d}n−1/d curse for fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ, while the prefactor deteriorates as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0.

Proof Sketch

By the envelope theorem, the fluctuation of Lcϵ\mathcal L_c^\epsilonLcϵ​ with respect to its first marginal is controlled by the class of entropic dual potentials. The soft ccc-transform smooths these potentials at spatial scale ϵ\sqrt\epsilonϵ​ for a quadratic-type cost. Covering a bounded ddd-dimensional domain at this scale gives an effective complexity of order ϵ−d/2\epsilon^{-d/2}ϵ−d/2. Standard Rademacher or Dudley entropy bounds then give an empirical-process fluctuation of order ϵ−d/2/n\epsilon^{-d/2}/\sqrt nϵ−d/2/n​ for each marginal. Applying the same estimate to the three terms defining the debiased divergence gives the stated bound.

Sample Complexity of Estimating OT Maps¶

The preceding estimates concern transport values. For map estimation, one solves the empirical dual problem for potentials (fn,mϵ,gn,mϵ)∈Rn×Rm(\mathbf f_{n,m}^\epsilon,\mathbf g_{n,m}^\epsilon)\in\RR^n\times\RR^m(fn,mϵ​,gn,mϵ​)∈Rn×Rm, with ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0 denoting the unregularized Kantorovich problem, and then uses the soft ccc-transform as an out-of-sample extrapolator.

For the quadratic cost c2(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2c_2(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2/2c2​(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2, let Pn,mϵ=(Pijϵ)P_{n,m}^\epsilon=(P_{ij}^\epsilon)Pn,mϵ​=(Pijϵ​) be the empirical entropic coupling and let gn,mϵ\mathbf g_{n,m}^\epsilongn,mϵ​ be the target-side dual potential. Define

un,mϵ(x)=−ϵlog⁡∑jbjexp⁡(gn,m,jϵ−c2(x,Yj)ϵ),Tn,mϵ(x)=x−∇un,mϵ(x).u_{n,m}^\epsilon(x) = -\epsilon\log \sum_j b_j \exp\left( \frac{\mathbf g_{n,m,j}^\epsilon-c_2(x,Y_j)}{\epsilon} \right), \qquad T_{n,m}^\epsilon(x)=x-\nabla u_{n,m}^\epsilon(x).un,mϵ​(x)=−ϵlogj∑​bj​exp(ϵgn,m,jϵ​−c2​(x,Yj​)​),Tn,mϵ​(x)=x−∇un,mϵ​(x).
(17)

Equivalently, subtracting the quadratic marginal terms turns c2c_2c2​ into the bilinear cost cip(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩c_{\rm ip}(x,y)=-\langle x,y\ranglecip​(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩. With the sign convention used here, the associated soft convex potential is

φn,mϵ(x)=12∥x∥2−un,mϵ(x)=ϵlog⁡∑jbjexp⁡(⟨x,Yj⟩+gn,m,jϵ−12∥Yj∥2ϵ),Tn,mϵ=∇φn,mϵ.\varphi_{n,m}^\epsilon(x) = \frac12\norm{x}^2-u_{n,m}^\epsilon(x) = \epsilon\log\sum_j b_j \exp\left( \frac{\langle x,Y_j\rangle+\mathbf g_{n,m,j}^\epsilon-\frac12\norm{Y_j}^2}{\epsilon} \right), \qquad T_{n,m}^\epsilon=\nabla\varphi_{n,m}^\epsilon .φn,mϵ​(x)=21​∥x∥2−un,mϵ​(x)=ϵlogj∑​bj​exp(ϵ⟨x,Yj​⟩+gn,m,jϵ​−21​∥Yj​∥2​),Tn,mϵ​=∇φn,mϵ​.
(18)

Differentiating this log-sum-exp gives the explicit soft barycentric form

Tn,mϵ(x)=∑jωjϵ(x)Yj,ωjϵ(x)=bje(gn,m,jϵ−c2(x,Yj))/ϵ∑kbke(gn,m,kϵ−c2(x,Yk))/ϵ.T_{n,m}^\epsilon(x)=\sum_j\omega_j^\epsilon(x)Y_j, \qquad \omega_j^\epsilon(x)= \frac{b_j e^{(\mathbf g_{n,m,j}^\epsilon-c_2(x,Y_j))/\epsilon}} {\sum_k b_k e^{(\mathbf g_{n,m,k}^\epsilon-c_2(x,Y_k))/\epsilon}} .Tn,mϵ​(x)=j∑​ωjϵ​(x)Yj​,ωjϵ​(x)=∑k​bk​e(gn,m,kϵ​−c2​(x,Yk​))/ϵbj​e(gn,m,jϵ​−c2​(x,Yj​))/ϵ​.
(19)

Tn,mϵ(Xi)=1ai∑jPijϵYj,T_{n,m}^\epsilon(X_i)=\frac1{a_i}\sum_jP_{ij}^\epsilon Y_j,Tn,mϵ​(Xi​)=ai​1​j∑​Pijϵ​Yj​,
(20)

which is the barycentric projection of the entropic plan. For ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0, the soft transform becomes the hard ccc-transform and the same formula uses an optimal unregularized empirical plan. The consistency statement below is written for uniform empirical weights, which is the standard statistical setting; deterministic nonuniform weights are handled by the same compactness argument with the corresponding grid-entropy bound.

Proposition: Consistency of Empirical Barycentric Maps

Let Ω⊂Rd\Omega\subset\RR^dΩ⊂Rd be compact, let α,β∈P2(Ω)\alpha,\beta\in\Pp_2(\Omega)α,β∈P2​(Ω), and assume that α\alphaα is absolutely continuous. The analogous backward statement holds when β\betaβ is also absolutely continuous.

Proof Sketch

Compare the entropic minimizer with an unregularized empirical optimal plan. On a uniform n×mn\times mn×m grid, the relative entropy with respect to α^n⊗β^m\hat\alpha_n\otimes\hat\beta_mα^n​⊗β^​m​ is at most log⁡(nm)\log(nm)log(nm), so the entropic coupling has asymptotically optimal quadratic cost when ϵlog⁡(nm)→0\epsilon\log(nm)\to0ϵlog(nm)→0. Any weak limit is therefore an optimal population plan, hence the Brenier graph (Id⁡,T)#α(\operatorname{Id},T)_\#\alpha(Id,T)#​α. Jensen’s inequality applied to each conditional law reduces the claim to the convergence of ∬∥y−T(x)∥2 dPn,mϵ(x,y)\iint\norm{y-T(x)}^2\,dP_{n,m}^{\epsilon}(x,y)∬∥y−T(x)∥2dPn,mϵ​(x,y). This last convergence is not a continuity tautology, because the Brenier map is only defined α\alphaα-a.e. At every differentiability point of ϕ\phiϕ, the subdifferential is the singleton {∇ϕ(x)}\{\nabla\phi(x)\}{∇ϕ(x)}; compactness of the target bounds the selected subgradients, and the closed-graph property of the subdifferential then gives continuity of any selected subgradient there. Since convex functions are differentiable Lebesgue-a.e. and α\alphaα is absolutely continuous, the portmanteau theorem for bounded test functions continuous almost everywhere under the limiting measure gives the desired limit.

Quantitative map rates require stronger stability assumptions on Brenier potentials. For unregularized map estimation, Hütter--Rigollet, Deb--Ghosal--Sen, and Manole--Balakrishnan--Niles-Weed--Wasserman obtain, under smoothness and curvature assumptions, squared L2(α)L^2(\alpha)L2(α) risk of order

E∥T^n−T0∥L2(α)2≲n−2s2(s−1)+d\mathbb E\norm{\widehat T_n-T_0}_{L^2(\alpha)}^2 \lesssim n^{-\frac{2s}{2(s-1)+d}}E∥∥​Tn​−T0​∥∥​L2(α)2​≲n−2(s−1)+d2s​
(22)

up to logarithms, and this rate is minimax optimal Hütter & Rigollet, 2021Deb et al., 2021Manole et al., 2021. For the Sinkhorn-computable entropic barycentric estimator, Pooladian--Niles-Weed prove

E∥Tϵ,(n,n)−T0∥L2(α)2≲ϵ−d/2log⁡(n)n−1/2+ϵ(sˉ+1)/2+ϵ2I0(α,β),\mathbb E\norm{T_{\epsilon,(n,n)}-T_0}_{L^2(\alpha)}^2 \lesssim \epsilon^{-d/2}\log(n)n^{-1/2} + \epsilon^{(\bar s+1)/2} + \epsilon^2\mathcal I_0(\alpha,\beta),E∥∥​Tϵ,(n,n)​−T0​∥∥​L2(α)2​≲ϵ−d/2log(n)n−1/2+ϵ(sˉ+1)/2+ϵ2I0​(α,β),
(23)

with sˉ=s∧3\bar s=s\wedge3sˉ=s∧3 Pooladian & Niles-Weed, 2021. The first term is the statistical fluctuation of the entropic map, while the last two terms are regularization-bias terms. Thus fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ gives a parametric empirical fluctuation for the regularized map, whereas ϵ≃n−1/(d+sˉ+1)\epsilon\simeq n^{-1/(d+\bar s+1)}ϵ≃n−1/(d+sˉ+1) gives a convergent estimator of the Brenier map. The unregularized case can achieve sharper minimax rates when combined with enough smooth extension machinery; the regularized estimator is instead directly Sinkhorn-computable.

Remark: No free lunch when approximating exact OT

The parametric rate in Proposition Proposition: Sinkhorn Divergences Interpolate the Rates holds for fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ. If the goal is to approximate the unregularized OT value, one must also account for the regularization bias. In a typical bounded-cost finite-dimensional regime,

∣Lˉcϵ(α,β)−Lc(α,β)∣≤Cϵ,E∣Lˉcϵ(α^n,β^n)−Lˉcϵ(α,β)∣≤Cc,dϵ−d/2n−1/2.\abs{\bar\MK_\c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-\MK_\c(\alpha,\beta)} \leq C\epsilon, \qquad \EE\abs{\bar\MK_\c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_n)-\bar\MK_\c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)} \leq C_{c,d}\epsilon^{-d/2}n^{-1/2}.∣∣​Lˉcϵ​(α,β)−Lc​(α,β)∣∣​≤Cϵ,E∣∣​Lˉcϵ​(α^n​,β^​n​)−Lˉcϵ​(α,β)∣∣​≤Cc,d​ϵ−d/2n−1/2.
(24)

Balancing the two terms gives ϵ≃n−1/(d+2)\epsilon\simeq n^{-1/(d+2)}ϵ≃n−1/(d+2) and total error of order n−1/(d+2)n^{-1/(d+2)}n−1/(d+2). Equivalently, target accuracy η\etaη requires choosing ϵ≃η\epsilon\simeq\etaϵ≃η and n≃η−(d+2)n\simeq\eta^{-(d+2)}n≃η−(d+2) samples under this bound. Thus entropic smoothing improves the statistical behavior at fixed scale, but approximating exact OT still forces a bias-variance tradeoff whose exponent deteriorates with dimension.

Bias and Variance of OT¶

The previous section answered a coarse but essential question: how many samples are needed before an empirical OT quantity is accurate, typically up to universal constants. We now ask for a finer statistical description. Rather than only estimating the size of the error, we seek the first expansion of the plug-in estimator. Given empirical laws α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ and β^m\hat\beta_mβ^​m​, and an OT functional TTT, this expansion separates the leading statistical bias

Bn,m(T):=ET(α^n,β^m)−T(α,β)B_{n,m}(T) \eqdef \mathbb E T(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-T(\alpha,\beta)Bn,m​(T):=ET(α^n​,β^​m​)−T(α,β)
(25)

and the centered fluctuation

Zn,m(T):=T(α^n,β^m)−ET(α^n,β^m),Z_{n,m}(T) \eqdef T(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\mathbb E T(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m),Zn,m​(T):=T(α^n​,β^​m​)−ET(α^n​,β^​m​),
(26)

for OT functionals such as T(α,β)=Wpp(α,β)T(\alpha,\beta)=\Wass_p^p(\alpha,\beta)T(α,β)=Wpp​(α,β), T(α,β)=Lc(α,β)T(\alpha,\beta)=\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)T(α,β)=Lc​(α,β), or their entropic analogues. This is not just the central limit theorem of Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem, which describes the random signed measure n(α^n−α)\sqrt n(\hat\alpha_n-\alpha)n​(α^n​−α) itself. Here the empirical process is pushed through a nonlinear, often nonsmooth, transport value. The resulting law is governed by the local differentiability of the OT functional and by the geometry of its optimal dual potentials.

Literature Map¶

The shape of the limit depends sharply on the analytic regularity of the transport value. For exact OT on a finite or countable space, the map from empirical weights to optimal cost is convex and piecewise affine. Sommerfeld and Munk Sommerfeld & Munk, 2018, and the countable-space extensions of Tameling--Sommerfeld--Munk and Hundrieser--Klatt--Munk--Tameling Tameling et al., 2017Hundrieser et al., 2022, show that the natural limit is a directional delta-method limit: often a support function of a Gaussian process over an optimal dual face, rather than a Gaussian random variable. For Euclidean costs, del Barrio--Loubes and collaborators obtain central-limit theorems for empirical transportation costs under regularity and uniqueness assumptions on the Kantorovich potentials Barrio & Loubes, 2017Barrio et al., 2021. Entropic regularization makes the problem smoother. For fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, the value is differentiable with respect to the marginals, and the limiting variance is read directly from the entropic dual potentials. This is the point of view developed by Bigot--Cazelles--Papadakis, Klatt--Tameling--Munk, Hundrieser--Klatt--Munk, and Mena--Weed Bigot et al., 2019Klatt et al., 2020Hundrieser et al., 2021Mena & Weed, 2019. More recent results clarify weak limits beyond smooth costs and second-order null limits for Sinkhorn divergences González-Sanz & Hundrieser, 2023Goldfeld et al., 2022. These asymptotic statements do not replace the dimension-dependent bounds of Sample Complexity; they explain what the leading random object is, what constants appear, and where the bias comes from.

Bias Versus Centered Fluctuation¶

The decomposition

T(α^n,β^m)−T(α,β)=ET(α^n,β^m)−T(α,β)⏟bias+T(α^n,β^m)−ET(α^n,β^m)⏟centered fluctuationT(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-T(\alpha,\beta) = \underbrace{\mathbb E T(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-T(\alpha,\beta)}_{\text{bias}} + \underbrace{T(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\mathbb E T(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)}_{\text{centered fluctuation}}T(α^n​,β^​m​)−T(α,β)=biasET(α^n​,β^​m​)−T(α,β)​​+centered fluctuationT(α^n​,β^​m​)−ET(α^n​,β^​m​)​​
(27)

is elementary, but in OT it is genuinely diagnostic because the two terms may live on different scales. For the self-distance T(α^n,α)=Wpp(α^n,α)T(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)=\Wass_p^p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)T(α^n​,α)=Wpp​(α^n​,α), the population value is zero and the deterministic bias EWpp(α^n,α)\mathbb E\Wass_p^p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)EWpp​(α^n​,α) is the leading term. On a regular d′d'd′-dimensional support, the high-dimensional matching scale is n−p/d′n^{-p/d'}n−p/d′ when d′>2pd'>2pd′>2p, with a critical logarithmic correction when d′=2pd'=2pd′=2p. Below this threshold the rate is controlled by empirical-process fluctuations and can be faster; in one dimension, smooth positive densities give the familiar quantile-process asymptotics for Wpp\Wass_p^pWpp​, of order n−p/2n^{-p/2}n−p/2 for p>1p>1p>1, and in particular n−1n^{-1}n−1 for W22\Wass_2^2W22​. Thus p/d′p/d'p/d′ is the high-dimensional matching exponent, not a universal rate formula Dudley, 1969Fournier & Guillin, 2015Weed & Bach, 2019. By contrast, when T(α,β)T(\alpha,\beta)T(α,β) is nonzero and the OT functional is differentiable at (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)(α,β), the centered fluctuation is often governed by an ordinary n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 central limit theorem. A ``slow OT statistic’’ can therefore have three distinct causes: a large empirical bias, a nonsmooth directional limit, or a regularization bias Tϵ(α,β)−T0(α,β)T_\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-T_0(\alpha,\beta)Tϵ​(α,β)−T0​(α,β) that still has to be removed.

On the complementary event, Taylor’s formula applies in the relative interior: the first-order term is centered and the Hessian is locally bounded, so the plug-in bias is O(N−1)O(N^{-1})O(N−1). The variance convergence follows from the same expansion and from bounded moments of the multinomial fluctuation. The two-sample formula follows by applying the argument independently to the two marginals.

For the entropy-only convention LCϵ\mathcal L_\C^\epsilonLCϵ​ used in Entropic Regularization for Discrete Measures, the marginal entropy derivatives described after Proposition: First variations of entropic OT must be added to the potentials. For the debiased Sinkhorn divergence Lˉcϵ\bar\MK_c^\epsilonLˉcϵ​, the derivative is instead the difference between cross and self entropic potentials. At the null α=β\alpha=\betaα=β, this first derivative can vanish for the debiased statistic, and second-order limits then become relevant Goldfeld et al., 2022. This is a useful warning: the asymptotic law is determined not only by a rate, but also by the local geometry of the functional.

Three Error Terms When Entropy Estimates Exact OT¶

If the target is the exact cost T0(α,β)=Lc(α,β)T_0(\alpha,\beta)=\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)T0​(α,β)=Lc​(α,β) but the statistic uses TϵT_\epsilonTϵ​, three errors should be kept separate:

Tϵ(α^n,β^m)−T0(α,β)=Tϵ(α,β)−T0(α,β)⏟regularization bias+ETϵ(α^n,β^m)−Tϵ(α,β)⏟statistical bias+Zn,m(Tϵ)⏟centered fluctuation.T_\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-T_0(\alpha,\beta) = \underbrace{T_\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-T_0(\alpha,\beta)}_{\text{regularization bias}} + \underbrace{\mathbb E T_\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-T_\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)}_{\text{statistical bias}} + \underbrace{Z_{n,m}(T_\epsilon)}_{\text{centered fluctuation}} .Tϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)−T0​(α,β)=regularization biasTϵ​(α,β)−T0​(α,β)​​+statistical biasETϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)−Tϵ​(α,β)​​+centered fluctuationZn,m​(Tϵ​)​​.
(45)

This identity is trivial algebraically but important statistically. It is usually read after choosing ϵ=ϵn\epsilon=\epsilon_nϵ=ϵn​. For fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ, the statistical bias is typically O(n−1+m−1)O(n^{-1}+m^{-1})O(n−1+m−1) in finite dimension, and the centered fluctuation is OP(n−1/2+m−1/2)O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2})OP​(n−1/2+m−1/2); boundary events where an empirical finite histogram has a zero entry have exponentially small probability when the population weights are positive. The regularization bias disappears only when ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0, whereas the variance constants usually deteriorate as ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow0ϵ↓0. This is the asymptotic form of the bias--variance tradeoff illustrated in Div.

What Changes in Continuous Spaces¶

The finite-dimensional formulas above are not merely toy models; they are the cleanest template for the general mechanism. Whenever an OT value is Hadamard differentiable and admits a unique sufficiently regular dual potential f⋆f^\starf⋆, the empirical-process CLT and the delta method give a first-order Gaussian limit with one-sample variance Var⁡α(f⋆(X))\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(f^\star(X))Varα​(f⋆(X)). When differentiability fails, as can happen for exact OT because the dual optimizer is not unique or because one studies the degenerate self-distance T(α,α)=0T(\alpha,\alpha)=0T(α,α)=0, the limit may be non-Gaussian or may occur at a slower non-parametric scale. Entropic regularization smooths the dual potentials and typically restores a conventional first-order CLT for fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ, even under weak assumptions on the cost. If the target is unregularized OT, however, this statistical expansion must still be balanced against the bias Tϵ(α,β)−T0(α,β)T_\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-T_0(\alpha,\beta)Tϵ​(α,β)−T0​(α,β). Thus Sample Complexity gives dimension-dependent magnitudes, while the present section identifies the local asymptotic constants and covariance formulas needed for inference.

Sketching Sinkhorn in Linear Time¶

The statistical results above explain why entropic OT is attractive at fixed temperature, but they also expose a computational tension. Sampling the marginals replaces the input laws by empirical measures and reduces the problem to finitely many support points; subsampling or coarsening these supports is governed by the sample-complexity estimates of this chapter. Even after the supports are fixed, however, a Sinkhorn sweep still costs O(nm)O(nm)O(nm), because it repeatedly applies the Gibbs kernel to vectors. Kernel sketching attacks this second bottleneck: it keeps the sampled marginals fixed and samples, or otherwise compresses, the feature representation of the kernel used by Sinkhorn. The drawback of this sketching approach is that the additional approximation error induced by the kernel sketch is dimension-dependent, so the number of features needed for a fixed accuracy typically grows with the ambient dimension.

PSD Kernels and Ordinary Feature Sketches¶

The RKHS/MMD section, Dual RKHS Norms and Maximum Mean Discrepancies, already used positive semidefinite kernels to define Hilbertian discrepancies between measures. Recall that a symmetric kernel k:X×X→Rk:\Xx\times\Xx\to\RRk:X×X→R is positive semidefinite if, for every finite family (xi)i=1n(x_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​)i=1n​, the Gram matrix (k(xi,xj))ij(k(x_i,x_j))_{ij}(k(xi​,xj​))ij​ is positive semidefinite. Many scalable kernel methods start from an integral feature representation

k(x,y)=∫Z⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp dρ(z),ϕ:X×Z→Rp,k(x,y)=\int_Z \dotp{\phi(x,z)}{\phi(y,z)}_{\RR^p}\,d\rho(z), \qquad \phi:\Xx\times Z\to\RR^p,k(x,y)=∫Z​⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp​dρ(z),ϕ:X×Z→Rp,

(47)

This is the classical random-feature principle. For data points (xi)i=1n(x_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​)i=1n​, the dense Gram matrix K=(k(xi,xj))ijK=(k(x_i,x_j))_{ij}K=(k(xi​,xj​))ij​ is replaced by K~=ΦΦ⊤\widetilde K=\Phi\Phi^\topK=ΦΦ⊤, where Φ∈Rn×rp\Phi\in\RR^{n\times rp}Φ∈Rn×rp is the sampled feature matrix with entries Φi,(ℓ,q)=r−1/2ϕq(xi,zℓ)\Phi_{i,(\ell,q)}=r^{-1/2}\phi_q(x_i,z_\ell)Φi,(ℓ,q)​=r−1/2ϕq​(xi​,zℓ​), 1≤ℓ≤r1\leq \ell\leq r1≤ℓ≤r, 1≤q≤p1\leq q\leq p1≤q≤p. The number rrr of sampled latent variables is thus a second sample size, distinct from the number of data points. At this stage no positivity of ϕ\phiϕ is assumed; signed or oscillatory features are exactly what make Fourier sketches useful.

For translation-invariant kernels on Rd\RR^dRd, Bochner’s theorem gives the standard Fourier sketch. If k(x,y)=κ(x−y)k(x,y)=\kappa(x-y)k(x,y)=κ(x−y) and κ(t)=∫ei⟨ω,t⟩ dΛ(ω)\kappa(t)=\int e^{i\dotp{\omega}{t}}\,d\Lambda(\omega)κ(t)=∫ei⟨ω,t⟩dΛ(ω), with Λ\LambdaΛ a positive spectral measure, one may use real features ϕ(x,ω)=(cos⁡⟨ω,x⟩,sin⁡⟨ω,x⟩)\phi(x,\omega)=(\cos\dotp{\omega}{x},\sin\dotp{\omega}{x})ϕ(x,ω)=(cos⟨ω,x⟩,sin⟨ω,x⟩). For the Gaussian kernel kσ(x,y)=exp⁡(−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2))k_\sigma(x,y)=\exp(-\norm{x-y}^2/(2\sigma^2))kσ​(x,y)=exp(−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2)), this corresponds to ω∼N(0,σ−2Id)\omega\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2}\Id)ω∼N(0,σ−2Id). This random Fourier feature construction was introduced by Rahimi and Recht to accelerate large-scale kernel machines Rahimi & Recht, 2007; its statistical role for kernel ridge regression and related supervised methods is analyzed, for instance, in Rudi & Rosasco, 2017Avron et al., 2017.

The difficulty is that Sinkhorn is not a generic kernel method: it divides by K~v\widetilde K vKv and, in dual variables, applies logarithms. Thus one needs K~ij>0\widetilde K_{ij}>0Kij​>0, preferably with a relative error on the entries, because −ϵlog⁡Kij-\epsilon\log K_{ij}−ϵlogKij​ is the effective cost. This is a more stringent requirement than the usual spectral or Frobenius approximation of a PSD Gram matrix.

The next proposition is not a substitute for the sharp low-rank Sinkhorn theory. It is an elementary concentration lemma whose role is to isolate the two facts that matter for Sinkhorn: positivity of the approximate kernel and accuracy after taking logarithms. The full algorithmic statements rely on more refined Nyström or Gaussian-kernel approximations together with stability of Sinkhorn scaling Altschuler et al., 2018Altschuler et al., 2019.

This proposition pinpoints the obstruction. When ϵ\epsilonϵ is small or the data diameter is large, κ=min⁡Kij\kappa=\min K_{ij}κ=minKij​ can be exponentially small, so an ordinary signed sketch may need a very large rrr just to keep all entries positive. What Sinkhorn really needs is relative control of the kernel, equivalently additive control of the sketched costs. Positive features do not solve the whole approximation problem, but they remove the most basic failure mode: negative entries in K~\widetilde KK.

The dimension dependence is unavoidable in the worst case. For the quadratic cost on points contained in a radius-RRR ball of Rd\RR^dRd, the Nyström analysis of Altschuler, Bach, Rudi and Niles-Weed Altschuler et al., 2019 studies Kij=exp⁡(−η∥xi−xj∥2)K_{ij}=\exp(-\eta\norm{x_i-x_j}^2)Kij​=exp(−η∥xi​−xj​∥2) and bounds the effective rank by a quantity of the form

(59)

up to universal constants and harmless logarithms. Thus the resulting Sinkhorn computation is near-linear in nnn once this rank is fixed, but the required rank is polynomial in the inverse kernel bandwidth, with exponent ddd and only logarithmic dependence on nnn in this bound. When the same machinery is used to approximate unregularized quadratic OT to additive accuracy τ\tauτ, one takes η\etaη of order τ−1log⁡n\tau^{-1}\log nτ−1logn, so the complexity contains a factor τ−O(d)\tau^{-O(d)}τ−O(d), often summarized informally as an ϵ−d\epsilon^{-d}ϵ−d-type dependence on the target precision. The same work also explains why this can be much better on data with lower intrinsic dimension.

Positive Features and Total Positivity¶

A positive feature sketch asks for more than positive semidefiniteness. In finite dimension, let

DNNn={A∈Rn×n:A⪰0, Aij≥0},CPn={BB⊤:B∈R+n×q for some q≥1}.\mathrm{DNN}_n=\{A\in\RR^{n\times n}: A\succeq0,\ A_{ij}\geq0\}, \qquad \mathrm{CP}_n=\{BB^\top: B\in\RR_+^{n\times q}\hbox{ for some }q\geq1\}.DNNn​={A∈Rn×n:A⪰0, Aij​≥0},CPn​={BB⊤:B∈R+n×q​ for some q≥1}.
(60)

Matrices in DNNn\mathrm{DNN}_nDNNn​ are doubly nonnegative, while matrices in CPn\mathrm{CP}_nCPn​ are completely positive. One always has CPn⊂DNNn\mathrm{CP}_n\subset\mathrm{DNN}_nCPn​⊂DNNn​, with equality for n≤4n\leq4n≤4 and strict inclusion for n≥5n\geq5n≥5 Berman & Shaked-Monderer, 2003Anstreicher et al., 2009. Checking membership in the completely positive cone is computationally hard: strong membership is NP-hard, and weak membership for the completely positive cone and its copositive dual is NP-hard Dickinson & Gijben, 2014.

For kernels, it is useful to distinguish the two corresponding notions. A kernel kkk is doubly positive if every finite Gram matrix belongs to DNNn\mathrm{DNN}_nDNNn​, i.e. if kkk is PSD and pointwise nonnegative. It is totally positive in the positive-feature sense if every finite Gram matrix belongs to CPn\mathrm{CP}_nCPn​. This terminology should not be confused with Karlin’s classical total positivity, which concerns nonnegativity of all minors of an ordered kernel Karlin, 1968; it is a complete-positive-type condition, studied for instance in DeCorte et al., 2022.

The positive-feature construction of Scetbon and Cuturi Scetbon & Cuturi, 2020 makes the reason for this definition direct. If

k(x,y)=∫Z⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp dρ(z),ϕ(x,z)∈R+p,k(x,y)=\int_Z\dotp{\phi(x,z)}{\phi(y,z)}_{\RR^p}\,d\rho(z), \qquad \phi(x,z)\in\RR_+^p,k(x,y)=∫Z​⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp​dρ(z),ϕ(x,z)∈R+p​,
(61)

then every finite Gram matrix is a conic combination of rank-one matrices vv⊤vv^\topvv⊤ with v≥0v\geq0v≥0, and hence is completely positive. Conversely, on a fixed finite set, K∈CPnK\in\mathrm{CP}_nK∈CPn​ is exactly the existence of a nonnegative factorization K=BB⊤K=BB^\topK=BB⊤. Thus total positivity in this sense is precisely the kernel-level condition behind positive random features. For rectangular source--target matrices, one applies the same statement to the Gram matrix on the union of the sampled source and target points and then extracts its n×mn\times mn×m cross block.

Proposition: Basic Closure of Totally Positive Kernels

Nonnegative sums and pointwise products of totally positive kernels are totally positive. In particular, positive autocorrelations

k(x,y)=∫g(u−x)g(u−y) du,g≥0,k(x,y)=\int g(u-x)g(u-y)\,du, \qquad g\geq0,k(x,y)=∫g(u−x)g(u−y)du,g≥0,
(62)

and all nonnegative mixtures of such kernels are totally positive.

Proof

For sums, concatenate the nonnegative features and rescale them by the square roots of the nonnegative coefficients. For products, tensor the nonnegative features:

⟨ϕ1(x,z1),ϕ1(y,z1)⟩⟨ϕ2(x,z2),ϕ2(y,z2)⟩=⟨ϕ1(x,z1)⊗ϕ2(x,z2),ϕ1(y,z1)⊗ϕ2(y,z2)⟩.\dotp{\phi_1(x,z_1)}{\phi_1(y,z_1)} \dotp{\phi_2(x,z_2)}{\phi_2(y,z_2)} = \dotp{\phi_1(x,z_1)\otimes\phi_2(x,z_2)} {\phi_1(y,z_1)\otimes\phi_2(y,z_2)}.⟨ϕ1​(x,z1​),ϕ1​(y,z1​)⟩⟨ϕ2​(x,z2​),ϕ2​(y,z2​)⟩=⟨ϕ1​(x,z1​)⊗ϕ2​(x,z2​),ϕ1​(y,z1​)⊗ϕ2​(y,z2​)⟩.
(63)

The tensor feature remains entrywise nonnegative. The autocorrelation formula is already a positive feature representation with latent variable uuu and scalar feature g(u−x)g(u-x)g(u−x).

The Gaussian Gibbs kernels used by Sinkhorn admit an especially simple positive feature representation, which is the construction exploited by Scetbon and Cuturi Scetbon & Cuturi, 2020. The same construction extends to the generalized Gaussian kernels e−∥x−y∥p/ϵe^{-\norm{x-y}^p/\epsilon}e−∥x−y∥p/ϵ for 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2, because these kernels are mixtures of Gaussian kernels. This is the Schoenberg--Bernstein mechanism behind the positive definiteness of radial stable kernels Schoenberg, 1938Berg et al., 1984.

Let 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2, ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, and

kp,ϵ(x,y)=exp⁡(−∥x−y∥pϵ),x,y∈Rd.k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \exp\left(-\frac{\norm{x-y}^p}{\epsilon}\right), \qquad x,y\in\RR^d .kp,ϵ​(x,y)=exp(−ϵ∥x−y∥p​),x,y∈Rd.
(64)

E(e−tSa)=e−ta,t≥0,\mathbb E\left(e^{-tS_a}\right)=e^{-t^a}, \qquad t\geq0,E(e−tSa​)=e−ta,t≥0,

exp⁡(−taϵ)=∫0+∞e−λt dνa,ϵ(λ),t≥0.\exp\left(-\frac{t^a}{\epsilon}\right) = \int_0^{+\infty} e^{-\lambda t}\,d\nu_{a,\epsilon}(\lambda), \qquad t\geq0.exp(−ϵta​)=∫0+∞​e−λtdνa,ϵ​(λ),t≥0.
(66)

Equivalently, for a nonnegative random variable Λ∼νa,ϵ\Lambda\sim\nu_{a,\epsilon}Λ∼νa,ϵ​,

kp,ϵ(x,y)=EΛexp⁡(−Λ∥x−y∥2).k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \mathbb E_\Lambda\exp\left(-\Lambda\norm{x-y}^2\right).kp,ϵ​(x,y)=EΛ​exp(−Λ∥x−y∥2).
(67)

Fix a centering point x0∈Rdx_0\in\RR^dx0​∈Rd, let Z∼N(0,Idd)Z\sim\mathcal N(0,\Id_d)Z∼N(0,Idd​), independent of Λ\LambdaΛ, and set

qx(Λ)=2Λ (x−x0),ϕp(x,Λ,Z)=exp⁡(⟨Z,qx(Λ)⟩−∥qx(Λ)∥2).q_x(\Lambda)=\sqrt{2\Lambda}\,(x-x_0), \qquad \phi_p(x,\Lambda,Z) = \exp\left(\dotp{Z}{q_x(\Lambda)}-\norm{q_x(\Lambda)}^2\right).qx​(Λ)=2Λ​(x−x0​),ϕp​(x,Λ,Z)=exp(⟨Z,qx​(Λ)⟩−∥qx​(Λ)∥2).
(68)

Then

kp,ϵ(x,y)=EΛ,Z(ϕp(x,Λ,Z)ϕp(y,Λ,Z)).k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \mathbb E_{\Lambda,Z} \left(\phi_p(x,\Lambda,Z)\phi_p(y,\Lambda,Z)\right).kp,ϵ​(x,y)=EΛ,Z​(ϕp​(x,Λ,Z)ϕp​(y,Λ,Z)).
(69)

Thus kp,ϵk_{p,\epsilon}kp,ϵ​ is totally positive in the complete-positive sense. In particular, if (Λℓ,Zℓ)ℓ=1r(\Lambda_\ell,Z_\ell)_{\ell=1}^r(Λℓ​,Zℓ​)ℓ=1r​ are i.i.d. copies of (Λ,Z)(\Lambda,Z)(Λ,Z), then

k~p,ϵ(x,y)=∑ℓ=1rφℓ(x)φℓ(y),φℓ(x)=r−1/2ϕp(x,Λℓ,Zℓ),\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \sum_{\ell=1}^r \varphi_\ell(x)\varphi_\ell(y), \qquad \varphi_\ell(x)=r^{-1/2}\phi_p(x,\Lambda_\ell,Z_\ell),kp,ϵ​(x,y)=ℓ=1∑r​φℓ​(x)φℓ​(y),φℓ​(x)=r−1/2ϕp​(x,Λℓ​,Zℓ​),
(70)

is an unbiased nonnegative feature sketch of kp,ϵk_{p,\epsilon}kp,ϵ​.

For p=2p=2p=2, the mixing law reduces to the Dirac mass ν1,ϵ=δ1/ϵ\nu_{1,\epsilon}=\delta_{1/\epsilon}ν1,ϵ​=δ1/ϵ​, which recovers the usual Gaussian feature formula.

Proof

The function s↦e−sas\mapsto e^{-s^a}s↦e−sa is completely monotone for 0<a≤10<a\leq10<a≤1. Bernstein’s theorem therefore gives the Laplace-transform representation of a positive aaa-stable random variable SaS_aSa​. The scaling Λ=ϵ−1/aSa\Lambda=\epsilon^{-1/a}S_aΛ=ϵ−1/aSa​ gives

Ee−tΛ=exp⁡(−taϵ),\mathbb E e^{-t\Lambda} = \exp\left(-\frac{t^a}{\epsilon}\right),Ee−tΛ=exp(−ϵta​),
(71)

which is the displayed representation by νa,ϵ\nu_{a,\epsilon}νa,ϵ​. Applying this identity with t=∥x−y∥2t=\norm{x-y}^2t=∥x−y∥2 gives the Gaussian-mixture formula.

Conditionally on Λ=λ\Lambda=\lambdaΛ=λ, the Gaussian moment-generating function gives

EZ(ϕp(x,λ,Z)ϕp(y,λ,Z))=exp⁡(−∥qx(λ)∥2−∥qy(λ)∥2)EZ(exp⁡⟨Z,qx(λ)+qy(λ)⟩)=exp⁡(−12∥qx(λ)−qy(λ)∥2)=exp⁡(−λ∥x−y∥2).\begin{aligned} \mathbb E_Z\left(\phi_p(x,\lambda,Z)\phi_p(y,\lambda,Z)\right) &= \exp\left(-\norm{q_x(\lambda)}^2-\norm{q_y(\lambda)}^2\right) \mathbb E_Z\left(\exp\dotp{Z}{q_x(\lambda)+q_y(\lambda)}\right) \\ &= \exp\left(-\frac12\norm{q_x(\lambda)-q_y(\lambda)}^2\right) = \exp\left(-\lambda\norm{x-y}^2\right). \end{aligned}EZ​(ϕp​(x,λ,Z)ϕp​(y,λ,Z))​=exp(−∥qx​(λ)∥2−∥qy​(λ)∥2)EZ​(exp⟨Z,qx​(λ)+qy​(λ)⟩)=exp(−21​∥qx​(λ)−qy​(λ)∥2)=exp(−λ∥x−y∥2).​
(72)

Taking the expectation over Λ\LambdaΛ gives kp,ϵk_{p,\epsilon}kp,ϵ​. Since ϕp\phi_pϕp​ is positive, this is a positive-feature representation; hence every finite Gram matrix is completely positive. The Monte-Carlo sketch is just the empirical average of this representation.

Remark: The Range 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2

The restriction 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2 is essential. Schoenberg’s theorem says that x↦e−γ∥x∥px\mapsto e^{-\gamma\norm{x}^p}x↦e−γ∥x∥p is positive definite on every Euclidean space precisely in this range. For p>2p>2p>2, the generalized Gaussian kernel is not positive definite in general: there are finite Euclidean point clouds for which the Gram matrix has a negative eigenvalue. Thus no universal positive-feature factorization of the above type should be expected. Constants in the cost, such as using ∥x−y∥p/p\norm{x-y}^p/p∥x−y∥p/p, are absorbed by rescaling ϵ\epsilonϵ.

Choosing x0x_0x0​ near the data can reduce the dynamic range of the features without changing the kernel. More generally, Gaussian scale mixtures give many radial totally positive kernels, including standard covariance families used in Gaussian processes Rasmussen & Williams, 2006.

The gap between doubly positive and totally positive kernels is real. On the circle, consider

kλ(x,y)=λ+cos⁡2(x−y2),λ>0.k_\lambda(x,y)=\lambda+\cos^2\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right), \qquad \lambda>0.kλ​(x,y)=λ+cos2(2x−y​),λ>0.
(73)

This kernel is PSD and strictly positive pointwise, since cos⁡2(t/2)=(1+cos⁡t)/2\cos^2(t/2)=(1+\cos t)/2cos2(t/2)=(1+cost)/2 has nonnegative Fourier coefficients and λ\lambdaλ adds a positive constant mode. For λ=1/20\lambda=1/20λ=1/20, however, its Gram matrix on five equally spaced points is not completely positive. The Horn copositive matrix HHH satisfies ⟨H,B⟩≥0\langle H,B\rangle\geq0⟨H,B⟩≥0 for every completely positive matrix BBB, but the five-point Gram matrix KKK gives

⟨H,K⟩=214−552<0.\langle H,K\rangle = \frac{21}{4}-\frac{5\sqrt5}{2}<0.⟨H,K⟩=421​−255​​<0.
(74)

Thus K∈DNN5∖CP5K\in\mathrm{DNN}_5\setminus\mathrm{CP}_5K∈DNN5​∖CP5​, and the kernel is doubly positive but not totally positive.

Positive Sketches for Sinkhorn¶

For the ppp-power cost cp(x,y)=∥x−y∥pc_p(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^pcp​(x,y)=∥x−y∥p, with 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2, the Sinkhorn Gibbs kernel is the generalized Gaussian kernel

kp,ϵ(x,y)=exp⁡(−∥x−y∥pϵ).k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \exp\left(-\frac{\norm{x-y}^p}{\epsilon}\right).kp,ϵ​(x,y)=exp(−ϵ∥x−y∥p​).
(75)

The factor 1/p1/p1/p, often used in the definition of WppW_p^pWpp​, only rescales ϵ\epsilonϵ. For p≥1p\geq1p≥1, this is the usual ppp-Wasserstein power cost; for 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, it should be read simply as a concave power transport cost. Proposition Proposition: Generalized Gaussian Positive Features gives a positive factorization of this kernel. With rrr draws (Λℓ,Zℓ)∼νp/2,ϵ⊗N(0,Idd)(\Lambda_\ell,Z_\ell)\sim\nu_{p/2,\epsilon}\otimes\mathcal N(0,\Id_d)(Λℓ​,Zℓ​)∼νp/2,ϵ​⊗N(0,Idd​), define the normalized features

φℓ(x)=r−1/2ϕp(x,Λℓ,Zℓ),1≤ℓ≤r.\varphi_\ell(x)=r^{-1/2}\phi_p(x,\Lambda_\ell,Z_\ell), \qquad 1\leq \ell\leq r .φℓ​(x)=r−1/2ϕp​(x,Λℓ​,Zℓ​),1≤ℓ≤r.
(76)

They satisfy

k~p,ϵ(x,y)=∑ℓ=1rφℓ(x)φℓ(y)≥0,E[k~p,ϵ(x,y)]=kp,ϵ(x,y).\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \sum_{\ell=1}^r\varphi_\ell(x)\varphi_\ell(y) \geq0, \qquad \mathbb E[\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y)]=k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y).kp,ϵ​(x,y)=ℓ=1∑r​φℓ​(x)φℓ​(y)≥0,E[kp,ϵ​(x,y)]=kp,ϵ​(x,y).
(77)

The corresponding matrices (ΦX)iℓ=φℓ(xi)(\Phi_X)_{i\ell}=\varphi_\ell(x_i)(ΦX​)iℓ​=φℓ​(xi​) and (ΦY)jℓ=φℓ(yj)(\Phi_Y)_{j\ell}=\varphi_\ell(y_j)(ΦY​)jℓ​=φℓ​(yj​) give a positive factorization K~=ΦXΦY⊤\widetilde K=\Phi_X\Phi_Y^\topK=ΦX​ΦY⊤​. Sinkhorn can therefore be run safely on the sketched kernel, and the resulting plan is represented as

P~=diag⁡(u)ΦXΦY⊤diag⁡(v)=LR⊤,L=diag⁡(u)ΦX,R=diag⁡(v)ΦY.\widetilde P = \diag(u)\Phi_X\Phi_Y^\top\diag(v) = LR^\top, \qquad L=\diag(u)\Phi_X, \quad R=\diag(v)\Phi_Y .P=diag(u)ΦX​ΦY⊤​diag(v)=LR⊤,L=diag(u)ΦX​,R=diag(v)ΦY​.
(78)

The output is the exact entropic coupling for the sketched effective cost c~p,ϵ=−ϵlog⁡k~p,ϵ\widetilde c_{p,\epsilon}=-\epsilon\log\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}cp,ϵ​=−ϵlogkp,ϵ​, and it approximates the original WpW_pWp​-type entropic problem only insofar as this logarithmic kernel approximation is accurate. This route is complementary to worst-case near-linear Sinkhorn analyses Altschuler et al., 2017, low-rank Gaussian-kernel approximations for quadratic transport Altschuler et al., 2018, and factored-coupling models in which the coupling itself is constrained to have low rank Scetbon et al., 2021.

show_book_figure("sinkhorn-positive-feature-sketching")

Figure Notebook-code shows the object that is changed by this approximation. The top row shows the entropic couplings, while the bottom row shows the matching effective costs c~ϵ(x,y)=−ϵlog⁡k~ϵ(x,y)\widetilde c_\epsilon(x,y)=-\epsilon\log\widetilde k_\epsilon(x,y)cϵ​(x,y)=−ϵlogkϵ​(x,y) with black level sets. The dense Gaussian Gibbs kernel gives the usual entropic plan and the quadratic cost ∣x−y∣2|x-y|^2∣x−y∣2. A sufficiently rich rank-40 positive-feature sketch remains visually close to both, whereas rank-10 and rank-3 sketches still enforce the prescribed marginals after Sinkhorn scaling but progressively lose the geometric concentration of the true coupling because the logarithmic kernel approximation has become too coarse.

Connection with Linear Attention¶

The same algebra appears in transformer attention, studied later from a continuous-depth transport viewpoint in Evolution in Depth of Transformers. A softmax attention matrix has entries proportional to exp⁡(⟨qi,kj⟩)\exp(\dotp{q_i}{k_j})exp(⟨qi​,kj​⟩); linear-attention methods replace this positive kernel by features Φ(qi)⊤Φ(kj)\Phi(q_i)^\top\Phi(k_j)Φ(qi​)⊤Φ(kj​), so that attention can be applied as Φ(Q)(Φ(K)⊤V)\Phi(Q)(\Phi(K)^\top V)Φ(Q)(Φ(K)⊤V) rather than by forming the full n×nn\times nn×n matrix Katharopoulos et al., 2020Choromanski et al., 2021Wang et al., 2020Xiong et al., 2021. Sinkhorn sketching is the transport analogue of this idea: replace the Gibbs matrix by a positive feature factorization, keep only the scaling vectors and feature factors, and control the approximation in the logarithmic scale relevant to entropic potentials. The transport case is more constrained, however, since the approximate kernel is reused inside nonlinear normalizations until the prescribed marginals are reached for the sketched problem.
